title: Tight Stability Bounds for Robust Distributed Learning: Byzantine Failures Hurt Generalization More than Data Poisoning
claim: Under equal numbers of misbehaving workers, strong attacks on communication degrade generalization far more than data corruption, matching theoretical bounds.
layout: single line plot, increasing curves, dashed vertical threshold divider, legend top-left
description: A single line chart plots generalization error (y-axis, 0 to about 1.1) against the number of misbehaving workers (x-axis, 1 to 7). A legend in the upper left lists four series. Two navy lines with circle markers show empirical error under optimal data poisoning (solid) and the theoretical upper bound under data poisoning (dashed). The two navy lines nearly overlap and rise slowly to about 0.3. Two dark red lines with x markers show empirical error under a tailored Byzantine attack (solid) and a lower bound from Theorem 3.2 (dotted). The solid red line climbs steeply to about 1.1. The dotted red line starts at 5 workers and ends near 0.73. A black dashed vertical line at about 4.5 separates the regions f < n/3 and f ≥ n/3. The eye goes first to the diverging red and blue curves.
caption: Generalization Error Under Optimal Poisoning And Tailored Byzantine Attacks.
abstract: Robust distributed learning algorithms aim to maintain reliable performance despite the presence of misbehaving workers. Such misbehaviors are commonly modeled as \textit{Byzantine failures}, allowing arbitrarily corrupted communication, or as \textit{data poisoning}, a weaker form of corruption restricted to local training data. While prior work shows similar optimization guarantees for both models, an important question remains: \textit{How do these threat models impact generalization?} We show, for the first time, a fundamental gap in generalization guarantees between the two threat models: Byzantine failures yield strictly worse rates than those achievable under data poisoning. Our findings are based upon a tight algorithmic stability analysis of robust distributed learning.
